items.title: Headlines for November 06, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Democrats Lead in Alaska and Mississippi Senate Races as House Majority Approaches 260 Seats Nov 06, 2026 Democrats continue to build on their historic gains in Tuesday’s midterm elections as final results are tabulated. So far, Democrats have won 253 House seats compared to Republicans’ 157, with 25 races still undecided. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom has added to his narrow lead over incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. He’s currently ahead by more than 1,800 votes as election officials process provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots. Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Blanche K. Bruce was elected in 1875, during the Reconstruction era. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes, though a quarter of ballots remain to be counted. If Democrats win Alaska and Mississippi, their Senate caucus will grow to 56 members. ## Incoming Freshman Senators Call for New Leadership to Replace Top Democrat Chuck Schumer ... There are growing calls for new leadership to challenge Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed, Juliana Stratton and Adam Hamilton have all said they won’t support Schumer, as has Senate candidate Scott Colom in Mississippi. ... ## Pete Hegseth Defends Iran War, Demands $350B in Additional Funding and Vows to Fight Impeachment Nov 06, 2026 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended the Iran war and lashed out at his critics on Thursday, as the House of Representatives prepares to vote as early as next week on articles of impeachment. The effort to oust Hegseth is being led by Kentucky’s outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie, who gave Hegseth an ultimatum after Tuesday’s historic losses for Republicans: Resign or be removed by Congress. The effort appears to have enough bipartisan support to pass, after many Republican lawmakers turned on Hegseth following their party’s election rout. On Thursday, Hegseth posted a defiant video on social media in which he lavished praise on President Trump, demanded at least $350 billion in additional military funding, said transgender troops have a mental illness incompatible with military service, and claimed victory over diversity, equity and inclusion, which he called a “Marxist ideology built to destroy us.” And Hegseth vowed to fight against impeachment.

items.title: US inflation too high; essential to get back to 2%: Fed’s Williams By Reuters
items.excerpt: FRANKFURT, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US economic growth has remained resilient and the labour market is remarkably stable despite successive shocks, but inflation is too high and must be brought back to 2%, New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Friday. Inflation has soared across the world, mostly as the US war on Iran has pushed energy prices higher but also because soaring investment in AI has pushed up costs for some IT-related products and services. "Inflation is absolutely too high. It’s been too high for too long," Williams told a European Central Bank conference in Frankfurt. "It’s absolutely essential that we bring inflation back to our 2% target in a timely manner and a sustained basis." But Williams also argued that the Fed’s key focus should be on where inflation is heading and making sure that current shocks do not translate into broader or more persistent inflation. "Fortunately, we’re not seeing that happen so far in terms of inflation expectations, which remain well anchored," Williams said. "We’re seeing wage growth (that is), I think, consistent with our 2% goal." While Williams did not discuss what the Fed’s next policy move should be, he said the bank’s last policy statement had correctly concluded that it was appropriate for the Fed to collect more information to determine what the appropriate stance of policy is. Financial markets see a more than 50% chance of a rate hike by the Fed in December while a move by March is fully priced in.

items.title: Fed's Mary Daly says higher interest rates 'are likely to be needed' in inflation fight
items.excerpt: Published Fri, Nov 6 2026 1:39 PM EST Updated 2 Hours Ago ... - San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said in a CNBC interview Friday that she expects the central bank will have to raise benchmark interest rates further as it battles ... San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said Friday she expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further, but joined her fellow policymakers in saying the pace and timing remain uncertain. "My expectation is we're going to have to tighten policy further. Exactly when and how much is still to be decided because we just have to take all the variables that are coming in," Daly told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a live interview. "More is likely to be needed, and certainly ... I'm prepared to do that if that's what the economy calls for." The remarks came the same day the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October while the unemployment rate — the labor-market variable Fed officials focus on most — edged lower to 4.1%. Those numbers were substantially better than Wall Street expectations. Job creation, in fact, was nearly triple the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Daly called the report "good news for American workers," but noted the pressure inflation is exerting on household finances. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% annually in October, but the September inflation rate as measured by the consumer price index was 3.7%. "They see that they can get jobs, they continue to spend. They're not out of the game, but they are on a treadmill of high inflation," she said. "This has been high for too long, almost six years, and we're really starting to feel the burden of that spread everywhere." The policymaker said she's not concerned generally about economic growth but worried about the persistence of inflation. "The job market remains stable and solid, but not booming, and you see real wages falling because those wages are not really keeping up with inflation," Daly said. "I think that's the crux of this. Good news on the jobs front, not so clear that Americans are going to gain ground in the labor market." The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in September increased the central bank's benchmark overnight borrowing rate by a quarter percentage point to a target range of 3.75%-4%. However, the committee last week declined to follow up that hike with another move, saying it preferred to wait for "the accumulation of more information" before deciding its next move. Daly will vote on the committee next year and said she still favors a gradual approach. Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin said Thursday he also sees higher rates ahead but is unsure of the timeline.

items.title: U.S. continues to generate jobs, yet inflation is eroding Americans' spending power | PBS News
items.excerpt: Economy Nov 6, 2026 11:23 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. Hiring was far stronger than the 65,000 new jobs that economists had expected. The jobs report comes three days after voters delivered a stunning defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of Congress to the Democrats. But the latest jobs report looked solid. Labor Department revisions added a combined 84,000 new jobs to the August and September totals. The unemployment rate fell even though 421,000 people entered the labor force. Average hourly wages rose 0.4% in October from September, the biggest month-over-month gain since January. "This was a blowout jobs report," said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones. "Payroll growth exceeded expectations, revisions were positive, the unemployment rate fell, participation improved, and wage growth strengthened." The strong job gains will likely make Federal Reserve policymakers more confident in the health of the labor market, giving them leeway to focus on persistently high inflation and raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December. The central bank typically seeks to bring down inflation by lifting its key interest rate to cool borrowing and spending. The Fed raised the rate in September but left it alone at its meeting last month. Wall Street investors now see the chance of a December rate hike at 77%, up about 10 percentage points from Thursday, according to CME's FedWatch. "For sure, we're looking at another rate increase in December and possibly another one in early 2027," said Boston College economist Brian Bethune. Solid hiring also underscores a concern among many Fed officials that their key rate isn't high enough to slow inflation. Hourly wages were up a meager 3.1% from October 2025. That means many workers have seen their purchasing power decline over the past year, despite continued hiring. ... So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have added an average of 86,000 jobs a month. That is modest by historic standards but an improvement over 2025, when monthly job creation averaged 9,700. That was the weakest performance outside of a recession since 2002. Last year, high interest rates and President Donald Trump's unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring. ... The American economy and job market have proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks — Trump's double-digit tariffs on imports and the war with Iran, which has driven U.S. gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and pinched family budgets. Gross domestic product — the nation's output of goods and services — advanced at a sprightly 3.4% annual pace from July through September, lifted by strong consumer spending and booming investment in artificial intelligence.

items.title: Markets fret over growth and inflation despite easing oil prices By Reuters
items.excerpt: LONDON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Uncertainty over the growth outlook and expectations that inflation will remain elevated next year are weighing on global markets, even as hopes of a de-escalation in the Iran war have eased oil prices. Government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year, the tech-led Nasdaq racked up on Thursday its biggest one-day drop since April 2025’s Liberation Day rout and European economic data has softened. The combination is fuelling concern that inflation could stay high even as growth slows, although the Democratic victory in US midterm elections has raised hopes for an eventual end to the Iran war. OIL STILL HIGH Oil has fallen 15% this week to just below $100 a barrel. But analysts warn that any resolution to the Iran war remains uncertain, leaving scope for prices to rise again. Oil is still up 64% this year, while natural gas remains nearly three times its level at the start of 2026. That backdrop is keeping near-term inflation expectations elevated and reinforcing concerns that price pressures could persist as growth slows, forcing central banks to raise interest rates further. The University of Michigan’s measure of one-year US inflation expectations edged up to 4.7% in October from 4.6% in September and ​3.4% in February. Market measures of long-term inflation expectations remain above 2% in the euro zone and the US, and above 3% in Britain. Higher energy costs add to inflation while also weighing on growth by increasing transport, manufacturing and household expenses. AllianceBernstein chief investment strategist Inigo Fraser Jenkins said the geopolitical tensions and supply disruptions driving inflationary pressures would persist beyond the US midterms. "Today it’s oil, but next time it could be cobalt, lithium or something else, and we need to get used to that," he said. "It will manifest itself in the form of higher inflation and greater volatility." FOOD PRICES BITE Food prices, driven higher by extreme weather, shipping disruptions and elevated energy costs, remain a key inflation concern. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization’s Food Price Index is at its highest level in nearly four years. Costs could rise further, with major consumer goods and food companies warning of price increases to offset higher expenses, while Britain’s leading retail trade body has flagged similar concerns. Food inflation can also fuel broader economic pressures, said Hank Calenti, global markets strategist at SMBC. "Food inflation makes people start to think that ’there’s really inflation here and it’s going to stay high and I need to get a better job or my employer needs to pay me more’," he said. "So, those second-round effects come in."

items.title: Two top Justice Department officials resign as post-election exodus accelerates By Reuters
items.excerpt: Updated Nov 06, 2026, 12:12 PM ... By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Two top officials at the US Department of Justice resigned on Friday, accelerating an exodus of senior figures from the department following Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress. The departures of John Eisenberg, who headed the DOJ’s national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who pursued probes into the past criminal investigations of Trump, follow the resignation of civil rights unit chief Harmeet Dhillon on Thursday. The DOJ is now without leaders for two of its signature initiatives — relitigating past investigations and targeting higher education. It is not clear why Quiñones or Eisenberg resigned. It is not unusual for senior US officials to leave the government following a midterm election, especially one that delivers a sharp setback to the party in power. Democrats plan a raft of investigations into Trump’s administration and business dealings. As US attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Quiñones was at the center of Trump’s attempts to leverage the Justice Department to investigate his political adversaries. His office was tasked with investigating the criminal probes of Trump’s handling of classified documents after he left office in 2021 and his campaign’s contacts with Russia in the 2016 election, among other issues. The investigation, which officials dubbed a “grand conspiracy”, sought to establish that the president was the victim of a long-running criminal conspiracy. But it has struggled to bring criminal charges thus far and the prosecutor who had been overseeing the probe, Joseph diGenova, resigned in September. Quiñones’ Miami office also brought criminal charges against former Cuban President Raul Castro in a major escalation of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign against the communist country.

items.title: Headlines for November 06, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Democrats Lead in Alaska and Mississippi Senate Races as House Majority Approaches 260 Seats Nov 06, 2026 Democrats continue to build on their historic gains in Tuesday’s midterm elections as final results are tabulated. So far, Democrats have won 253 House seats compared to Republicans’ 157, with 25 races still undecided. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom has added to his narrow lead over incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. He’s currently ahead by more than 1,800 votes as election officials process provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots. Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Blanche K. Bruce was elected in 1875, during the Reconstruction era. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes, though a quarter of ballots remain to be counted. If Democrats win Alaska and Mississippi, their Senate caucus will grow to 56 members. ## Incoming Freshman Senators Call for New Leadership to Replace Top Democrat Chuck Schumer Nov 06, 2026 There are growing calls for new leadership to challenge Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed, Juliana Stratton and Adam Hamilton have all said they won’t support Schumer, as has Senate candidate Scott Colom in Mississippi. This is Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed speaking with The Bulwark after Tuesday’s election. > Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed: “I’ve had conversations, obviously, with Senator Schumer in the context of this race. I’ve been clear: I want new leadership, and I want leadership that is focused on getting money out of politics, putting money in your pocket, passing Medicare for All. But at the end of the day, it’s a choice between two or more options, so I want to see who else is willing to put their hat in the ring.” On Wednesday, CNN’s Manu Raju asked Senator Schumer about growing calls for him to step down as Senate Democratic leader. > Manu Raju: “How do you deal with those candidates who won who say they’re not going to vote for you?” > Sen. Chuck Schumer: “Look” — > Manu Raju: “Adam Hamilton, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed?” > Sen. Chuck Schumer: “OK, again, to repeat the answer: The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader.” In Texas, Senator-elect James Talarico has refused to commit to backing Schumer. Talarico is also calling on fellow Democrats to abolish the filibuster, a rule that effectively requires 60 of the Senate’s 100 members to pass legislation. Talarico spoke with NBC News. > Sen.-elect James Talarico: “I believe that the majority has the right to govern in this country. And the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution — it’s a Jim Crow relic — it is — it is leading to gridlock.” Meanwhile, an online petition calling on Democrats to reject New York Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries as House speaker in the new Congress has garnered over 830,000 signatures. ## Pete Hegseth Defends Iran War, Demands $350B in Additional Funding and Vows to Fight Impeachment Nov 06, 2026 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended the Iran war and lashed out at his critics on Thursday, as the House of Representatives prepares to vote as early as next week on articles of impeachment. The effort to oust Hegseth is being led by Kentucky’s outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie, who gave Hegseth an ultimatum after Tuesday’s historic losses for Republicans: Resign or be removed by Congress. The effort appears to have enough bipartisan support to pass, after many Republican lawmakers turned on Hegseth following their party’s election rout. On Thursday, Hegseth posted a defiant video on social media in which he lavished praise on President Trump, demanded at least $350 billion in additional military funding, said transgender troops have a mental illness incompatible with military service, and claimed victory over diversity, equity and inclusion, which he called a “Marxist ideology built to destroy us.” And Hegseth vowed to fight against impeachment. > Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth: “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me.”

items.excerpt: 25 years after 'Britney,' 5 new Britney Spears songs showcase a pop icon at a transformative moment NEW YORK (AP) — Britney Spears' 2001 self-titled album ‘Britney' marked a pivotal moment in her career. At 19, she was already a global icon, transitioning from teen pop to a more mature sound. The album, certified quadruple platinum, showcased her evolution with hits like “I'm A Slave 4 U.” On Friday, Legacy Recordings releases the “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition)." It features five previously unreleased tracks and two new remixes. These songs add depth to her legacy, reflecting themes of autonomy and self-definition. Fans can revisit the album, exploring its impact and Spears’ journey from adolescence to adulthood. ... Awkwafina digs into her culinary roots to try something a little crazy: Open a restaurant NEW YORK (AP) — Awkwafina has taken a surprising turn in her career by diving into the culinary world. Her new Apple TV series, “Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook,” follows her journey from a novice cook to opening her own restaurant. The show, premiering Friday, captures her learning experiences, from making stir-fry to mastering Peking duck. Awkwafina was born Nora Lum and comes from a family with a rich restaurant history. They opened the New York City eatery Lum's. Her journey reconnects her with her roots and honors her family. The series also highlights a trend of Asian Americans returning to the restaurant industry, defying their parents' expectations. 'ER' and 'The Pitt' are similar enough for lawsuit to move forward, appeals court finds LOS ANGELES (AP) — A California appeals court has found enough similarity between “ER” and “The Pitt” for a lawsuit by Michael Crichton's widow to proceed. The court ruled that the trial judge was correct to reject Warner Bros. Television's motion to dismiss. Both shows star Noah Wyle as an emergency room doctor and focus on the healthcare system. The lawsuit argues “The Pitt” is an unauthorized “ER” reboot. Crichton had a contract preventing any “ER” spinoffs without his consent. The court dismissed claims against Wyle and others, finding no evidence they interfered with Crichton's contract. In ‘Possible Love,’ a South Korean auteur returns with a story of marriage, labor and class VENICE, Italy (AP) — South Korean filmmaker Lee Chang-dong's latest film, “Possible Love,” is now streaming on Netflix. The film explores the impact of mass layoffs in South Korea, inspired by the 2009 Ssangyong Motor Co. incident. The story follows a laid-off autoworker and his wife, played by Jeon Do-yeon, who agrees to be followed by a well-off documentary filmmaker. The film, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival where it won the runner-up prize, is South Korea’s submission for the Academy Awards. Lee last directed “Burning,” which was short-listed for an Oscar in 2018. Lady Gaga, Shakira, Jack White and Boy George lead the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame nominees NEW YORK (AP) — Lady Gaga, Shakira, Pink, Boy George, Jack White, Sia, Vince Gill, Ne-Yo, Blondie’s Debbie Harry and Chris Stein are among the impressive list of nominees for the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame class. Also on the ballot are America’s Gerry Beckley and Dewey Bunnell, Grandmaster Melle Mel as well as members of ZZ Top and War. Eligible voting members have until midnight Eastern Standard Time on Dec. 14 to turn in ballots with their choices of up to three nominees from the songwriter category and up to three from the performing-songwriter category. The 2027 inductees will be announced in early 2027. Last year's class included Taylor Swift, Kiss’s Gene Simmons, Paul Stanley and more. Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand has been convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. The British comedian faces a significant prison term when sentenced Monday. Brand, known for his risqué comedy and past promiscuity, denied the charges. He was taken into custody after the judge rejected a bail request. Prosecutors described him as a manipulative predator. The jury deliberated for over eight hours before reaching the verdict. Brand was acquitted of two rape counts and one attempted indecent assault. Police have provided prosecutors with investigations into two more allegations against him. Brand's conviction follows a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4.
